are higher-growth Phase 2 adjacencies, each expanding from existing platforms, local presence, and workflow integration.

The central condition is execution discipline: the case weakens if workflow adoption is treated as an instrument sale rather than a managed multi-year assay, consumables, software, and service relationship.
Five opportunities ranked by workflow fit, recurring-revenue potential, and execution sequence
◆ PCR Instrumentation for Clinical Diagnostic Laboratories in the United States
Thermo Fisher combines molecular-testing instruments, PCR consumables, reagents, and clinical-laboratory relationships into an integrated workflow that reagent-only suppliers struggle to match.
◆ Liquid Chromatography Systems for Pharmaceutical and Biotechnology Companies in the United States
Thermo Fisher’s analytical-instrument portfolio, service coverage, and consumables model embed it in regulated pharmaceutical workflows where requalification raises switching costs.
◆ Microbiology Testing for Food and Beverage Processing Plants in Germany
The Sure Tect PCR System and beverage-spoilage multiplex assay offer a specific contamination-control workflow supported by Thermo Fisher’s European distribution and service footprint.
◆ Automated Liquid Handling Systems for Biopharmaceutical CDMOs in India
Thermo Fisher can bundle liquid handling, pipette tips, microplates, reagents, and services through its Indian operating presence and biopharma-services expertise.
◆ Preimplantation Genetic Testing for Fertility Clinics in Japan
Ion Torrent sequencing, PGT assays, automation, reporting software, and an established Japanese presence create a differentiated end-to-end fertility-laboratory workflow.

The portfolio is deliberately balanced. The two US opportunities are near-term growth anchors because they extend established customer access and service infrastructure. Germany strengthens a differentiated, consumables-led quality-control position. India creates a scalable automation adjacency tied to recurring labware and reagent demand. Japan offers longer-term exposure to specialized genetic-testing workflows where integrated platforms can carry meaningful switching costs.
Build recurring workflows first, then use international platforms to extend the installed base
1. PCR Instrumentation for Clinical Diagnostic Laboratories in the United States
PCR Instrumentation for Clinical Diagnostic Laboratories in the United States has a TAM of
. Its near-term appeal comes from pairing the installed molecular-testing footprint with recurring assays, PCR plates, consumables, and support rather than relying on one-time placement economics.
Why this can lead the portfolio
Clinical laboratories already recognize Thermo Fisher across molecular workflows, reducing the trust and validation burden associated with introducing a new platform.
The opportunity is strongest where infectious-disease, oncology, and decentralized molecular-testing needs justify an integrated instrument-plus-consumables workflow.

The defensibility comes from workflow embedding: assay configuration, laboratory standard operating procedures, staff familiarity, and reagent continuity make replacement more difficult after validation.
How the commercial model could work
Position the offer around workflow standardization, throughput reliability, and assay continuity instead of instrument specifications alone.
Use existing clinical-laboratory relationships to identify sites with fragmented PCR workflows, aging installed systems, or incomplete assay-menu coverage.
Attach service, reagent supply, plates, and workflow support during procurement so the customer relationship compounds after the initial placement.
What must be proven before scaling
Validate that laboratories adopt a meaningful recurring consumables mix rather than using the platform only for limited test menus.
Confirm that implementation capacity can support clinical validation timelines without creating a service bottleneck.
Watch for reimbursement or volume pressure that shifts buyer decisions toward lowest-cost testing rather than integrated workflow value.
2. Liquid Chromatography Systems for Pharmaceutical and Biotechnology Companies in the United States
Liquid Chromatography Systems for Pharmaceutical and Biotechnology Companies in the United States has a TAM of

. This is a high-quality expansion because regulated pharmaceutical quality-control and development laboratories value uptime, traceability, method reproducibility, and audit readiness alongside instrument performance.
Thermo Fisher can bring instruments, columns, consumables, software, and service together in a way that lowers operational handoffs for pharmaceutical and biotechnology laboratories.
Method transfer, validation documentation, and service continuity can create durable switching costs once the system is embedded in regulated quality-control processes.
This opportunity is economically stronger in accounts where lifecycle service and consumables are purchased with the system rather than sourced separately.
Where the entry motion is strongest
The best initial targets are pharmaceutical and biotechnology laboratories with expanding quality-control capacity, method-development backlogs, or complex compliance requirements.
Commercial teams can lead with lifecycle economics: validated uptime, consistent methods, consumables availability, and audit-ready support.
The sales motion should connect analytical-instrument specialists with service and consumables teams, because value capture depends on the entire workflow.
Competitive displacement becomes harder when an incumbent’s methods and installed systems are deeply entrenched.
The core proof point is whether Thermo Fisher can win on integrated lifecycle value rather than discounting hardware.
A weak after market attachment rate would reduce the strategic value even if instrument placements grow.
3. Microbiology Testing for Food and Beverage Processing Plants in Germany
Microbiology Testing for Food and Beverage Processing Plants in Germany has a TAM of

. The opportunity is narrower than the US platforms, but it has a clear customer problem: preventing spoilage events, protecting production uptime, and improving confidence in contamination-control workflows.
The Sure Tect beverage-spoilage multiplex assay gives Thermo Fisher an application-specific point of entry rather than a generic microbiology proposition.
Food and beverage producers have a direct operational incentive to detect contamination earlier because production disruption, waste, and brand exposure can be costly.
A validated assay workflow can generate recurring reagent and consumable demand as testing becomes embedded in plant quality operations.
How to get into the account
Begin with beverage and food-processing facilities where spoilage prevention is visible to both quality leaders and plant operations.
Use the European channel and service footprint to support a controlled pilot model that proves sensitivity, workflow fit, and turnaround performance.
Convert successful pilots into standard operating procedures, then expand across additional sites within the same processing group.
Adoption may stall if the workflow is perceived as adding complexity without a clear reduction in false positives, downtime, or testing delays.
Local application support is essential because plant quality teams will evaluate the assay against established microbiology practices.
The earliest warning sign is pilot usage without routine-test conversion; that would indicate technical interest but insufficient operational value.
4. Automated Liquid Handling Systems for Biopharmaceutical CDMOs in India
Automated Liquid Handling Systems for Biopharmaceutical CDMOs in India has a TAM of
. This Phase 2 opportunity is attractive because automation can pull through pipette tips, microplates, reagents, service, and workflow support across a growing biopharma manufacturing base.
Why the bundle is the advantage
Thermo Fisher can position liquid handling as part of a reproducible sample-preparation and assay workflow, not as a stand-alone automation platform.
Existing Indian operations reduce entry friction and make it more feasible to coordinate distribution, applications support, and service logistics.
The consumables attachment opportunity can make the relationship more durable than a capital-equipment sale alone.
How to stage the market entry
Concentrate early activity on CDMOs with visible workflow-scale requirements, quality-system maturity, and recurring assay volumes.
Use reference installations to demonstrate reproducibility, error reduction, and standardized consumables performance in local operating conditions.
Scale only after field applications support and service-response capacity can protect the installed base.
Complex implementation needs can overwhelm a sales-led rollout if local applications specialists and service coverage are not sequenced first.
Customers may defer automation if they cannot quantify labor, throughput, or error-reduction benefits against their existing manual processes.
A weak consumables pull-through rate would signal that the workflow has not become operationally embedded.
5. Preimplantation Genetic Testing for Fertility Clinics in Japan
Preimplantation Genetic Testing for Fertility Clinics in Japan has a TAM of
. This is a specialized Phase 2 platform opportunity where the strategic value rests on integrated sequencing, assays, automation, reporting software, and laboratory reproducibility.
The Ion Repro Seq PGT-A kit, Ion Gene Studio systems, assay portfolio, automation capabilities, and reporting software create a connected workflow for fertility laboratories.
Fertility clinics and partner diagnostic laboratories may value reproducibility, throughput, and reporting consistency more than isolated component performance.
Once workflows are validated and staff are trained, assay and software continuity can create meaningful operational stickiness.
Build through specialized fertility laboratories and diagnostic partners that can act as reference accounts and workflow-validation sites.
Lead with reproducibility and laboratory throughput while aligning clinical, technical, and commercial stakeholders around the complete workflow.
Treat regulatory interpretation and reimbursement sensitivity as design inputs to the market model, not as issues to address after launch.
Confirm that clinics perceive enough differentiated value to support the workflow’s cost and implementation requirements.
Establish whether reimbursement and regulatory conditions permit sustained testing volumes in the target account set.
The thesis changes if adoption remains confined to research use or if specialized competitors retain stronger clinician confidence.
Execution quality and workflow adoption are more important than headline market size
